To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the basal forebrain (BF) neurons project to the visual cortex (VC) in the rat as early as birth, that BF neurons projecting to VC have a well‐developed morphology at birth, and that BF neurons projecting VC increase in size, complexity, and spine density during the first 2 weeks of life.
the BFB neurons project to the visual cortex as early as birth and that the BFB axons and their terminals develop during the first postnatal weeks.

1) the BFB neurons that project to the visual cortex are located in the diagonal band, medial septum, and substantia inominata, and 2) BFB neurons projecting to the visual cortex develop dendritic arbors and spine density during the first 2 weeks of postnatal life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ontogeny of the BFB projections to visual cortex.
the development of basal ganglia‐cortical connections in the rat.
the development of the visual cortex in rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BFB neurons project to visual cortex in the rat as early as the first postnatal day and that these projections develop in a manner similar to other cortical inputs.
the visual cortex is innervated by the BFB as early as the first postnatal day.
the BFB is a source of projections to the developing rat visual cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
BFB projections to the visual system appear to develop in a similar manner as BFB projections to other cortical areas.
BFB projections to the visual system develop in the first few postnatal weeks and that the development is not dependent upon sensory experience.
BFB projections to visual cortex are established at birth, and BFB neurons are well developed at that time.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the BFB neurons projecting to occipital cortex are present and well differentiated at the beginning of the critical period, and that their development does not depend on activity from occipital cortex.
BFB neurons project to the visual cortex early in development, and their dendritic arbors and spine densities increase with age.
the development of BFB projections to the visual system is not simply a case of the BFB projecting to the developing cortex and then pruning its axons.
